messages.subject: Trouble with storing peakPick object
parts:
Hi all,

I am completely new to R, so this might be a stupid question. I am playing around with cardinal using a dataset containing 44032 features and 4981 pixels. When I run the peakPick function on the data set at pixel=1 everything works fine and a plot is generated. When I try the same function on the whole dataset and storing the results into a new object I get the following error:

> data2 <- peakPick(data, method="simple", SNR=3)
peakPeak: Using method = simple
  |============================================================================================| 100%
Error in validObject(object) : 
  invalid class “MSImageData” object: 1: number of non-NA indices in positionArray must match number of cols of data elements
invalid class “MSImageData” object: 2: number of non-NA indices in positionArray must match number of rows of coord

There appears to be a mismatch between the matrices of data and data2? Do I have to make changes to my data matrix prior to running pickPeak?

Any help is greatly appreciated!

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: Trouble with storing peakPick object
parts:
Hi Vadim,

Can you try running :

any(duplicated(coord(data)))

If it returns TRUE, then you somehow have duplicated pixel coordinates.

If that is the case, a quick fix (which throws away pixel with duplicated coordinates) would be:

data <- data[,!duplicated(coord(data))]

-Kylie

messages.author: fbe93367c39d0e3f
messages.subject: Re: Trouble with storing peakPick object
parts:
Hi Kylie,

Turns out I did have duplicates in the data set and was able to get ride of them with the command you posted. Storing generated objects works perfectly now. Thank you!

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: Trouble with storing peakPick object
parts:
Hi Vadim,

Good to hear it works. The main reason I've encountered this is when coordinates are stored as decimals rather than integers. Cardinal implicitly rounds them to integers, since it expects a regular pixel grid, so some pixels may be rounded to share coordinates that were different by a decimal.  If there is a reason you need more control over the pixel coordinates, you may want to write your own function to transform the coordinates to integers more correctly.

-Kylie

I will experiment to see if rounding produces significant data loss and biases the analysis.
